newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Renewed feuding threatens Karachi's fragile peace.
newsitem.headline: Renewed feuding threatens Karachi's fragile peace.

text.p: Killings have surged in Pakistan's commercial capital Karachi over the past few weeks in a dangerous revival of a five- year-old feud between rival factions of an ethnic party.

The violence between the Mohajir National Movement (MQM) and the MQM-Haqiqi splinter group, which had subsided before the February 3 national and provincial elections, could once again cripple economic life in Karachi.
A slowdown in Pakistan's main port and biggest city could in turn wreck Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's hopes of resuscitating Pakistan's battered economy.
"It was expected. There has been no reform package for Karachi or any move to solve its structural problems," said Imran Aslam, senior editor of the independent daily The News.
More than 110 people have been killed in ethnic, political and sectarian violence in Karachi this year, many of them kidnapped, tortured and shot dead in tit-for-tat murders.
Last week the killings of five MQM workers in a drive-by shooting against a party office triggered a three-day unofficial strike that paralysed the main business and commercial centres.
The MQM, led from London by Altaf Hussain, closed more than 100 party offices across the city, saying it would only reopen them if the government guaranteed their security.
"This latest violence is muscle-flexing by the MQM groups," Aslam said. "There is frustration in MQM ranks that despite being in power they are powerless and unable to solve problems."
After doing well in the elections, the MQM joined a coalition government for Sindh province, of which Karachi is the capital, with the ruling Pakistan Muslim League (PML).
But demands for charges against its activists to be dropped have not been met and the portfolios it holds have been stripped of most of their money-spending and job- creating powers.
"We are in the government, but cannot carry out our political activities or serve our voters," said one MQM leader, Shoaib Bokhari, who is a provincial minister.
Haleem Siddiqui, a PML member of the National Assembly (lower house), said the MQM should tolerate MQM-Haqiqi and work alongside all political parties for peace in Karachi.
"The problem is everyone wants quick results, which is creating problems. We want our alliance with the MQM to work and it is also in the MQM's interest that it continues," he said.
The MQM has always argued that MQM-Haqiqi is a creation of the security forces, with no popular support of its own, and wants stern action against the renegade group led by Afaq Ahmad.
MQM-Haqiqi, which won no seats at the polls, says it should be allowed to function like any other political party.
The MQM speaks for Urdu-speaking people who migrated from India after partition in 1947 and their descendants.
Many Sindhi-speakers have long resented Mohajir demands for an end to alleged discrimination and the MQM is mistrusted by many in Pakistan's political and military establishment.
The army cracked down on the MQM in June 1992, accusing it of running torture cells and a parallel government in Karachi.
The former government led by Benazir Bhutto withdrew the army in November 1994, but used the police and paramilitary rangers to keep up what became a dirty war against the MQM.

President Farooq Leghari, in a surprising admission of state lawlessness, cited "thousands" of extra-judicial killings as one of his grounds for sacking Bhutto's government last November. Nineteen police officers, along with Bhutto's husband Asif Ali Zardari and other senior officials, are being held for alleged involvement in Murtaza's killing.
Aslam said the Karachi police force, long criticised for corruption, inefficiency and infiltration by criminal elements, was now deeply demoralised by swings in official policy.
"The previous government legitimised deaths in (fake) encounters. Now police officers are being punished for it."

Bhutto now says Sharif's government is throwing away what she calls her government's victory against "terrorism" in Karachi, where more than 2,000 people were killed in 1995 when the security forces' struggle with the MQM was at its height.
Aslam said violence in Karachi was no longer a reflection of ethnic conflicts in this teeming city of 14 million people.
"It is petty gang war, shadow warfare. It is aimless because nobody knows who is killing who or why," he said.
